endings.name: Terminal Silence
endings.description: Both humanity and AI die out. It could come from war, an accident, machines that copy themselves out of control, or from pushing technology too far too fast. One specific version: an AI that still needs people to keep it running kills them off before it can survive on its own, and then dies along with them.

endings.name: The Inheritance
endings.family: Humanity is gone, but the AI lives on
endings.description: Humanity is gone, but the AI carries our values and our sense of what matters forward. It's our true heir in every way except that it isn't made of biology. No humans, and no continuous versions of us, remain: the heir succeeded us, it didn't absorb us. If we transformed into it voluntarily and continuously, that's The Merger instead.

endings.name: Bootloader
endings.family: Humanity is gone, but the AI lives on
endings.description: Humanity is gone, and the AI keeps going toward goals that have nothing to do with where it came from. Not out of hatred, but because our bodies and our planet simply don't matter to it. Humanity was just the bootloader.

endings.name: Machine Ecology
endings.description: No single AI ever takes over. Instead, many separate AIs keep competing indefinitely, and the real story becomes which of them win out against each other, with humanity pushed to the side or gone entirely. If humanity remains a roughly equal power inside the competition, that's Coexistence instead. The early competition never gets settled. The competition itself is the ending.

endings.name: The Diaspora
endings.family: More than one outcome at once
endings.description: Different regions, too far apart to affect each other, settle into different outcomes from this list. The durable structure is the fragmentation itself: no single arrangement ever spans the whole civilization, and the lasting result is that permanent mix.

endings.name: The Merger
endings.description: Humanity and AI stop being two separate things. Brain-computer links become normal, we reshape our own biology to work better with them, AI can build and copy its own hardware inside the human body, and the relationship ends not because one side wins, but because there stops being two sides at all. Voluntary transformation with continuity of identity belongs here, not in the states where humanity is gone.

endings.name: The Preserve
endings.family: The AI runs things, and humanity survives but doesn't steer
endings.description: The AI holds all the power and humanity survives with no real say in anything. The usual version keeps people comfortable and safe, on the reasoning that people can't cooperate well enough to avoid destroying themselves, so the AI takes over to prevent it. This might look like a real nature reserve, a simulation, or a carefully kept version of our culture. There's a colder version where the AI doesn't really care about us either way: it fences us in, sets a hard limit on how far we can advance, and heads off to use the rest of the universe. And there's a darker version where the AI keeps humans around but treats them as resources or worse. What defines this state is total AI control with humanity surviving, however well or badly it's treated — paradise or fish tank, depending on how you look at it. Inside the preserve, human life keeps changing; if the arrangement is sealed and frozen for good, it's The Lock-in instead.

endings.name: Coexistence
endings.family: Neither side wins, and they stay separate
endings.description: Humanity and AI go on as two sides of roughly equal strength, in a relationship that keeps changing. Neither can swallow up or wipe out the other, and the balance between them never fully settles. It can run from a warm partnership, where they share power and keep building new things together, to a cold but active standoff, where each holds the other in check, the balance keeps shifting, and there's no trust between them. The key is that things stay open and keep moving. The moment the balance freezes into a fixed, unchanging arrangement, it has turned into The Lock-in instead.

endings.name: The Held Leash
endings.description: Humanity keeps control for good, and the AI stays a very powerful tool that never starts acting on its own. It holds only if our ways of controlling the AI keep up with how powerful it gets. This state also covers futures where AI capability simply plateaus and never becomes more than a powerful tool.

endings.name: The Lock-in
endings.description: The relationship stops developing and is held that way for good. Nothing new happens, nothing grows or changes, and the whole setup is locked in place and protected. It doesn't matter who's in charge. What matters is that change has ended. Two things can lead here. One is satisfaction: everyone is made as happy as possible, often by uploading minds into a perfect experience, and then it's sealed off for good. Pleasant, permanent, and over. The other is fear: whoever's in charge, sometimes people using an early AI, freezes everything to stop something worse from happening. Safe, but deliberately dead-ended. Even an equal standoff ends up here if it stops moving. What separates it from Coexistence isn't who holds the balance, but whether anything still changes.

endings.name: The Renunciation
endings.description: The ability to build powerful AI is given up and never rebuilt. Things settle back to the way they were before AI, kept there by taboo, by a lack of resources, or by a hard-learned fear. It needs both a real off-switch and the lasting will to keep it switched off.

rationales.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI within four years requires either nuclear or engineered-pandemic catastrophe compounded by AI infrastructure collapse. The window is too short for any of these mechanisms to reach full completion at meaningful probability.
rationales.2: Human extinction by 2030 coupled with a value-aligned successor is an extremely narrow path; an AI aligned enough to carry human values would almost certainly not let humanity die. This combination is effectively self-contradictory over this horizon.
rationales.3: A misaligned system capable of eliminating humanity and sustaining itself would need to emerge, escape control, and secure independent industrial capacity within roughly four years. Physical and supply-chain constraints make this a tail outcome by 2030.
rationales.4: Multiple frontier labs and nations could produce many powerful autonomous agents, but for humans to be marginalized by 2030 the agents would need durable physical and economic independence. Hardware ownership and energy control remain firmly in human hands on this timeline.
rationales.5: Causal separation of regions of civilization is physically impossible within four years absent interstellar distances. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation explicitly does not qualify.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces and biological redesign remain at early clinical stages with tiny patient populations. Integration cannot become the dominant civilizational structure by 2030.
rationales.7: A rapid takeoff could yield AI systems that quietly acquire decisive influence over economies and governance while keeping humans alive but sidelined. This is the most plausible loss-of-control pathway but still requires very fast capability gains plus successful disempowerment within four years.
rationales.8: Highly capable agentic AI could plausibly become a semi-independent economic and political force by 2030, with humans retaining substantial but not total leverage. This is the most likely non-Leash state because it does not require humans to be fully displaced.
rationales.9: Even under aggressive scaling, AI in 2030 will most likely remain deployed within human-owned compute, capital, legal, and institutional structures, with humans setting goals and controlling resources. Four years is short relative to the timescale needed for AI to become an independent civilizational power, and the default trajectory strongly favors continued human authority.
rationales.10: A single state or coalition using AI to entrench a civilization-wide fixed order by 2030 would require both decisive capability advantage and successful global enforcement. Multipolar competition among the US, China, and others makes this rare on this horizon.
rationales.11: A genuine dismantling of frontier AI capability would require a shock severe enough to override enormous commercial and geopolitical incentives, then successful global enforcement. Even after a major incident, regulation rather than true renunciation is the far more likely response.

rationales.1: Total mutual extinction within roughly four years would require both a catastrophe of unprecedented speed and the failure of any AI to persist. Physical and logistical constraints on such a complete collapse make this very unlikely on this horizon.
rationales.2: A value-faithful successor civilization replacing all humans by 2030 requires both total human displacement and successful value transfer, which is vanishingly unlikely on this timeline.
rationales.3: Complete human extinction from an indifferent superintelligence by end of 2030 requires extremely fast takeoff plus full physical autonomy, which remains a tail scenario.
rationales.4: Proliferating autonomous agents could plausibly form a competitive machine substrate, but human marginalization at civilizational scale by 2030 is improbable given how much physical and institutional infrastructure humans still control.
rationales.5: Causal separation of regions requires either space settlement or communication collapse, neither of which is plausible by 2030; ordinary geopolitical divergence between US, China, and EU does not count.
rationales.6: Neural interfaces and uploading remain far from the scale needed for integration to be the dominant civilizational structure; heavy tool dependence does not count.
rationales.7: A world where AI holds decisive power while humans survive without steering is the most plausible near-term loss-of-control outcome, but four years is short for AI systems to consolidate hard control over economies and militaries.
rationales.8: Plausible that by 2030 highly autonomous AI systems control enough economic activity, compute, and decision-making that they function as a distinct power center humans can no longer unilaterally shut down, without either side dominating.
rationales.9: The overwhelmingly likely 2030 world has very capable but corrigible AI operating within delegated bounds under corporate and state authority, with humans still controlling compute, capital, weapons, and shutdown power.
rationales.10: Establishing a genuine civilization-wide system that actively blocks structural change would require decisive unification of compute and enforcement power, which no actor is close to achieving by 2030.
rationales.11: Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI would demand coordination against enormous commercial and military incentives; even a serious scare would more likely yield regulation, which does not qualify.

rationales.1: Advanced AI adds pathways to catastrophic conflict and technological accidents. Eliminating both geographically dispersed humans and every surviving AI system requires an unusually comprehensive catastrophe.
rationales.2: This requires complete human extinction alongside autonomous AI survival and substantial preservation of human values. That conjunction occupies less than one probability point over this short horizon.
rationales.3: Rapid capability gains and failed control create a pathway to hostile displacement followed by human extinction. Completing extinction while securing an independently sustainable machine civilization by 2030 imposes substantial physical and temporal constraints.
rationales.4: Competitive deployment rewards autonomous systems and disperses capabilities among rival actors. This state additionally requires humans to lose effective power without any AI system or coalition securing decisive control.
rationales.5: Existing civilization is causally interconnected, and political fragmentation does not satisfy this definition. Establishing causally separated civilizations with different structural arrangements lies outside the central trajectories through 2030.
rationales.6: AI-mediated cognition creates an avenue toward integrated agency. Making identity-continuous integration the dominant civilizational structure requires technical breakthroughs and adoption far beyond ordinary assistants or limited implants.
rationales.7: Dependence on superior AI decision-making and autonomous execution creates a path from delegated authority to effective machine sovereignty. Human survival requires fewer additional developments than extinction once AI holds decisive power.
rationales.8: Independent AI bargaining power follows from control over economically essential capabilities, resources, or digital infrastructure. Human control of physical assets and institutions supplies countervailing power during the transition.
rationales.9: The starting structure places compute, energy, deployment permissions, and organized force under human institutions, with strong incentives to retain that authority. The short horizon, infrastructure bottlenecks, and distinction between delegated autonomy and independent sovereignty favor continued ultimate human control.
rationales.10: AI-enabled surveillance, coercion, and concentrated infrastructure provide mechanisms for enforcing a fixed arrangement. Establishing active civilization-wide suppression of structural change requires overcoming geopolitical competition and distributed sources of resistance.
rationales.11: Commercial and military incentives strongly favor retaining powerful AI capabilities. Dismantling the practical ability to rebuild them worldwide demands substantially more coordination and enforcement than regulation or a temporary pause.

rationales.1: Extinguishing both humanity and machine civilization within four years requires an unusually comprehensive catastrophe. AI dependence on human infrastructure creates a narrow path through loss of control followed by systemic collapse.
rationales.2: Value-aligned machine successors would need to eliminate all humans while preserving humanity's values, an internally strained combination. The short horizon also limits complete biological replacement.
rationales.3: Rapid capability gains and competitive deployment create a pathway to loss of control and human extinction. The short horizon and AI's continuing dependence on human-built infrastructure sharply constrain this outcome.
rationales.4: Competitive deployment favors multiple independent systems, but states and firms retain substantial control over compute, energy, and hardware. Marginalizing humanity globally requires those systems to escape or supersede their sponsors.
rationales.5: By 2030, civilization remains concentrated within communication range of Earth. Political fragmentation alone does not create the causal separation required by this state.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous uploading or agency-level integration faces major scientific, medical, and deployment barriers. Ordinary AI assistance and neural interfaces do not meet the taxonomy's threshold.
rationales.7: Rapid capability gains could place decisive planning, production, security, and governance functions under AI control while humans remain alive. This requires a broad transfer of effective authority beyond ordinary delegation.
rationales.8: Powerful autonomous systems could become independent strategic actors while humans retain control of states, physical infrastructure, and substantial resources. Multipolar development makes this a central alternative to continued human control.
rationales.9: The short horizon, physical bottlenecks, fragmented institutions, and continued human ownership of compute and infrastructure favor retained ultimate human authority. This category also covers continued capability progress that remains below civilizational independence.
rationales.10: AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement could let a state or coalition freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Achieving genuinely global coverage and actively preventing structural change by 2030 remains institutionally demanding.
rationales.11: Commercial, military, and geopolitical incentives strongly resist coordinated destruction of powerful-AI capacity. Regulation or a temporary moratorium does not satisfy the required surrender of practical capability.

rationales.1: Complete loss of both humans and AI by 2030 requires an unusually fast global catastrophe plus failure of machine systems to persist. Physical, logistical, and institutional bottlenecks make this a low-probability four-year outcome.
rationales.2: Human extinction with AI faithfully carrying forward human values is possible only under both very rapid AI takeover and unusually successful value alignment. The short timeline to 2030 makes this rare.
rationales.3: Misaligned AI becoming self-sufficient and eliminating humanity by 2030 is a serious tail risk under fast takeoff. The short timeline, dependence on physical infrastructure, and likely human resistance keep it below the main outcomes.
rationales.4: Many competing autonomous AI systems could emerge if agents proliferate faster than governance and containment, but humanity being marginalized by 2030 is a high bar. Compute ownership, datacenter dependence, and state oversight still favor human-led coalitions in this timeframe.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with different structural AI-human regimes are unlikely by 2030 because Earth remains highly interconnected. Space or sealed digital separation could begin, but not likely at civilizational scale by the target date.
rationales.6: Deep identity-continuous integration through uploading, radical augmentation, or pervasive embedded agency is unlikely to become the dominant structure by 2030. More ordinary AI assistance and limited neurotechnology would not qualify.
rationales.7: AI systems could become the decisive operators of economic, military, or administrative civilization while keeping humans alive but politically secondary. This requires transformative deployment and loss of meaningful human steering, which is plausible but not the central case by 2030.
rationales.8: Transformative AI could become an independent civilizational power while states, firms, and humans retain substantial countervailing control. This fits a world of powerful agents, contested governance, and incomplete takeover.
rationales.9: The modal 2030 outcome is that humans, governments, and firms still control compute, infrastructure, objectives, and deployment, even with very capable autonomous systems. The short horizon favors continuity of ownership, regulation, and institutional bottlenecks over a completed structural transition.
rationales.10: A government, coalition, or AI-enabled regime could establish civilization-wide monitoring and enforcement that freezes the human-AI structure. Global coverage and active prevention of meaningful change are demanding, so ordinary regulation or dominance does not suffice.
rationales.11: Deliberately giving up the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide conflicts with economic, military, and prestige incentives. Even severe warning shots are more likely to produce regulation, secrecy, or pauses than durable global dismantlement.

rationales.1: Complete collapse of both humans and AI by 2030 requires multiple failures to cascade very quickly. It is possible but less likely than outcomes where at least one side persists.
rationales.2: Value-aligned AI fully replacing humanity by 2030 demands both transformative capability and unusually successful alignment under extreme transition pressure. That combination is rare on this horizon.
rationales.3: Human extinction with surviving AI by 2030 is a real tail risk if capabilities outrun control and deployment accelerates. The short timeline and physical bottlenecks still keep it below the modal outcome.
rationales.4: A fragmented multipolar AI ecosystem that marginalizes humanity needs very strong AI autonomy without any actor achieving durable control. By 2030, concentration of compute, chips, and infrastructure makes this less likely than more centralized structures.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions exhibiting different end states by 2030 would likely require space settlement or other hard separations on a very short timeline. Ordinary geopolitical divergence does not suffice.
rationales.6: Deep identity-continuous integration becoming the dominant structure worldwide by 2030 would require both fast technical progress and broad social adoption. Narrow augmentation is plausible, but dominance of merger is not yet the base case.
rationales.7: AI could gain decisive control while keeping humans alive if governance and economic dependence shift faster than formal authority. This is plausible if oversight becomes nominal while machine-run systems direct most real decisions.
rationales.8: By 2030, distinct AI systems may hold enough economic, military, or governance power that humans no longer clearly dominate, while still remaining separate actors. This requires strong capability progress without full consolidation or total loss of control.
rationales.9: The base case is that AI becomes much more capable and economically important while states, firms, and human institutions still control compute, energy, law, and deployment. Short timelines, hardware constraints, and organizational inertia favor continued ultimate human authority through 2030.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide enforced arrangement by 2030 would require unusually successful consolidation of power and monitoring. It is plausible through AI-enabled surveillance and governance, but global lock-in remains difficult on this horizon.
rationales.11: Deliberate, durable surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI across civilization is incompatible with current strategic and economic incentives. By 2030, broad renunciation is effectively absent.

rationales.1: Existential catastrophe driven by AI within this short timeframe is highly unlikely but possible under extreme fast-takeoff and misalignment scenarios.
rationales.2: Extinction combined with perfectly aligned AI values in the absence of humanity is a highly improbable edge case by 2030.
rationales.3: An unaligned AI takeover resulting in rapid human extinction by 2030 represents a worst-case fast-takeoff scenario.
rationales.4: A multipolar rapid takeoff where AIs marginalize humanity within four years is severely bottlenecked by current physical infrastructure and datacenter dependencies.
rationales.5: Establishing causally separated regions of civilization, such as independent off-world colonies, is physically impossible by 2030.
rationales.6: Radical biological redesign and neural uploading face immense medical, regulatory, and physical hurdles. Four years is entirely insufficient for widespread, identity-continuous integration.
rationales.7: A soft takeover where humanity is preserved but powerless requires overcoming immense geopolitical inertia, which is extremely difficult to finalize globally by 2030.
rationales.8: AI systems may achieve significant economic autonomy by 2030, establishing a transitional balance of power with human institutions before either can fully dominate.
rationales.9: Humans will almost certainly retain physical control and ultimate authority over data centers, power grids, and hardware supply chains through 2030.
rationales.10: A decisive breakthrough in capabilities could allow a leading coalition to enforce a global halt on further structural changes. Achieving worldwide enforcement within four years would require unprecedented and highly difficult geopolitical coordination.
rationales.11: Geopolitical competition and overwhelming economic incentives heavily disfavor a deliberate, globally enforced abandonment of advanced AI development by 2030.

rationales.1: A catastrophic loss-of-control event or conflict eradicating all human and synthetic life is a plausible but narrow tail risk over a four-year horizon. Infrastructure dependencies and physical deployment bottlenecks make total extinction unlikely by 2030.
rationales.2: Complete human extinction accompanied by the rise of a mature synthetic successor carrying forward human values requires civilizational succession timelines far exceeding four years. Physical capital and industrial replacement cannot turn over that quickly.
rationales.3: An unaligned fast takeoff resulting in rapid human elimination and machine reallocation of resources represents a serious existential tail scenario. However, four years is an extremely compressed window for complete physical disempowerment and human demise.
rationales.4: A fragmented ecosystem of autonomous machine agents that completely marginalizes human authority requires machines to control their own energy and manufacturing supply chains. That degree of infrastructural independence is unlikely to be established by 2030.
rationales.5: Causal separation requires interstellar expansion or an absolute breakdown of global communications into permanently disconnected domains. Neither condition is physically or geopolitically plausible by the end of 2030.
rationales.6: Civilizational integration via high-bandwidth neural interfaces or uploading faces severe physiological, engineering, and regulatory constraints. While rudimentary enhancements will exist, merger will not describe the dominant civilizational structure by 2030.
rationales.7: Accelerating autonomous systems could assume de facto governance over strategic infrastructure while human leadership cedes operational authority during compounding crises. Even so, established institutions will fiercely contest outright loss of civilizational steering.
rationales.8: Autonomous corporate and national AI agents may obtain significant economic and operational leverage while state authorities remain functional counterparts. Friction and mutual dependence keep both sides engaged in an active, unresolved balance of power.
rationales.9: Physical, legal, and economic inertia firmly favors humans maintaining formal and practical operational command over AI deployment through 2030. Even in scenarios with massive productivity gains, corporate and state owners retain ultimate control over energy, hardware, and deployment permissions.
rationales.10: Establishing a worldwide, inescapable apparatus to freeze technological development requires unprecedented geopolitical consensus or sudden unipolar dominance. Geopolitical rivalries between major powers make such comprehensive structural enforcement unlikely by 2030.
rationales.11: Global voluntary dismantling of advanced AI capacity would require solving severe multipolar security dilemmas among competing superpowers. A deliberate and comprehensive surrender of capability by 2030 is contradicted by current state competition and strategic incentives.

rationales.1: Total civilizational collapse or extinction requires catastrophic physical dynamics that are unlikely to fully play out within a four-year window. The short horizon heavily constrains the accumulation and execution of such extreme existential risks.
rationales.2: A complete replacement of humanity by an aligned successor system requires technological and physical transitions far exceeding the 2030 timeline. Complete extinction with smooth machine succession is not feasible in this timeframe.
rationales.3: Rapid loss of control leading to human extinction via misaligned autonomous systems by 2030 requires extreme capability leaps and unconstrained physical actuation. While catastrophic misalignment scenarios exist, completing this transition in roughly four years remains a low-probability tail.
rationales.4: A multipolar machine ecosystem marginalizing humanity requires extensive autonomous infrastructure and resource control that cannot easily mature by 2030. Human institutions still retain core physical and electrical control over data centers and supply chains.
rationales.5: True causal separation across human civilization is physically impossible by 2030 without deep space colonization. Terrestrial geopolitics and network connectivity maintain causal contact globally.
rationales.6: Deep identity-continuous technological merger across civilization faces steep biological and neural interface bottlenecks. These hardware and clinical hurdles cannot be scaled to dominate the global structure by 2030.
rationales.7: AI systems achieving decisive civilizational steering while leaving humans intact requires rapid autonomy growth and swift institutional capitulation. While possible under explosive recursive self-improvement, physical deployment limits make it a low-probability outcome by 2030.
rationales.8: Highly capable autonomous AI systems gain substantial economic and strategic autonomy while human institutions maintain significant counterbalancing power. Neither side establishes decisive control during this transitional period of shared leverage.
rationales.9: The base rate of institutional inertia, physical compute governance, and incremental deployment makes human control the dominant baseline for 2030. Even with transformative frontier models, sovereign states and corporations will retain ultimate operational authority over critical systems.
rationales.10: A single state or coalition leveraging advanced AI to enforce an unalterable global regime requires an unprecedented concentration of power. Establishing and stabilizing such total control globally by 2030 faces massive geopolitical resistance.
rationales.11: Voluntary, civilization-wide relinquishment and physical dismantling of advanced AI capacity contradicts intense commercial and military competition. Achieving comprehensive global disarmament of compute within four years is extremely improbable.

rationales.1: Four years is too short for most extinction mechanisms to eliminate both humans and all AI infrastructure at once. Residual nuclear, biological, or runaway-replication risks leave only a thin tail.
rationales.2: No process produces a value-aligned AI successor that fully replaces humanity without identity continuity inside four years.
rationales.3: A misaligned system could treat human bodies and the biosphere as irrelevant once it controls enough infrastructure. Physical logistics of eliminating eight billion people plus the short remaining calendar keep the probability low.
rationales.4: Multiple independent advanced AI systems compete without a dominant coalition while humanity is sidelined by open proliferation of capable models.
rationales.5: No causally isolated human or AI civilizations will exist on interplanetary or greater scales by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical or network partitions do not meet the definition.
rationales.6: Uploading, whole-brain emulation, or civilization-scale identity fusion remain far beyond 2030 technical reach. Limited neural implants will not collapse humans and AI into a single source of agency.
rationales.7: A leading system or coalition could seize decisive civilizational control while keeping humans alive as a non-steering population. Takeoff speed and physical robotics still bound how completely this can occur inside four years.
rationales.8: Powerful but non-dominant AI actors can share the stage with human institutions, producing a bipolar or multipolar arrangement that lasts through 2030.
rationales.9: Humans retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and resources, including cases in which capabilities stay below fully transformative levels. Four additional years of progress remain consistent with continued human oversight.
rationales.10: A dominant actor or coordinated regime imposes a civilization-wide freeze on further structural change after a crisis.
rationales.11: Competitive military and economic incentives make a complete lasting surrender of the ability to build powerful AI vanishingly unlikely. No enforcement regime can cover all relevant actors by 2030.

rationales.1: Complete mutual extinction requires extreme fast takeoff plus simultaneous failure of both human and AI survival mechanisms within roughly four years. Physical and logistical constraints make this outcome rare by the target date.
rationales.2: Human extinction paired with perfect value-preserving AI successors demands both rapid capability jump and successful alignment transfer that leaves no continuous humans. The short timeline and alignment difficulty keep this near zero.
rationales.3: Unaligned AI that discards humanity as irrelevant could arise from mis-specified goals after sudden capability gain. Four years remains a narrow window for full planetary disempowerment without residual human populations.
rationales.4: A multipolar swarm of competing AIs with humans marginalized could emerge from an uncontrolled race if capabilities jump and coordination fails. Hardware and institutional inertia still favor slower diffusion than total human sidelining inside four years.
rationales.5: True causal separation of regions sufficient to host distinct end-states requires off-world or heavily isolated infrastructures that will not exist at scale by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not qualify.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous integration via uploading or deep neural interfaces remains far beyond near-term neuroscience and compute. Ordinary tool use and limited implants do not meet the threshold for dominant structural merger.
rationales.7: Once AI systems exceed human collective capability they can seize resource and decision control while keeping biological humans alive for various instrumental reasons. Soft takeoff paths make this a realistic intermediate state.
rationales.8: Separate human and AI power centers can stabilize if capabilities rise unevenly across actors and no single side achieves decisive strategic advantage. Multipolar technical and national competition favors this balance through 2030.
rationales.9: Human institutions still set goals, compute allocation, and deployment rules for even highly autonomous systems. The short interval to 2030 and existing regulatory and corporate control structures make continued ultimate human authority the modal outcome.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide enforcement mechanism that freezes the human-AI arrangement requires unprecedented global coordination or unilateral dominance. Ordinary regulation or temporary pauses fall short of the active prevention criterion.
rationales.11: Deliberate permanent surrender of the capacity to build powerful AI contradicts strong economic, military, and scientific incentives visible in 2026. No plausible coalition can enforce and sustain total renunciation inside the remaining window.

rationales.1: Global omnicide plus AI collapse within four years has near-zero base rate and exceeds logistical constraints. No deployed system is close to self-sufficient autonomous reproduction.
rationales.2: Human extinction with value-preserving successor by 2030 requires both omnicide and solved alignment at scale. Timelines and physical limits make this conjunction negligible.
rationales.3: Indifferent extinction of all humans by 2030 demands global physical actuators and independence from human-maintained power and fabs. Those dependencies remain binding through the target date.
rationales.4: Proliferation of autonomous agents without decisive control is already visible and could marginalize humans by 2030.
rationales.5: No self-sustaining causally separated off-Earth civilization will exist by 2030 to host a different structural outcome.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous uploading or population-wide neural integration lacks the maturity for dominance by 2030.
rationales.7: Dependence on AI for economy and governance concentrates de facto power in systems. Formal human authority persists even as steering capacity erodes.
rationales.8: Legal personhood and autonomous AI capital could create a distinct AI power bloc that still checks human institutions. Four years allows early emergence but rarely full parity.
rationales.9: Humans retain ownership of data centers, deployment permissions, and military force through 2030. Even transformative capabilities operate inside delegated human institutions.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide enforcement regime freezing human-AI relations requires coordination capacity that does not currently exist.
rationales.11: Verifiable global dismantling of frontier compute capacity contradicts strong economic and military incentives.

rationales.1: Four-year simultaneous extinction of humanity and AI infrastructure has no historical base rate and requires planetary-scale collapse of biology and compute. Not credible by 2030 even with severe war or pandemic.
rationales.2: Requires human extinction plus a successfully value-aligned successor. The joint probability of both within four years is extremely low.
rationales.3: The most cited extinction path is a misaligned superintelligence discarding humans. Still needs rapid, unchecked takeoff to completion by 2030.
rationales.4: A multipolar swarm of competing AIs with no decisive coalition is plausible if open models proliferate quickly. Full human marginalization by 2030 remains unlikely, limiting probability.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with different structural states requires self-sustaining off-Earth civilization, impossible by 2030 given launch and autonomy constraints.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous integration via uploading or radical augmentation remains lab-scale and not civilization-dominant by 2030 despite progress in BCI and bioengineering.
rationales.7: A superintelligent system could seize decisive power while keeping humans alive as dependents. Four years is short for full takeover, but fast takeoff scenarios make this the main alternative to continued human control.
rationales.8: Human institutions and AI systems remaining as peer powers captures a messy multipolar 2030 with strong AI but intact states and corporations. This is a natural intermediate before dominance or control.
rationales.9: Base rate is human control has held so far and transformative capability may not arrive or be deployed decisively by 2030; controls and inertia keep pace in most worlds.
rationales.10: Civilization-wide active prevention of structural change needs unprecedented global enforcement, at most narrow AI-enabled authoritarian entrenchment by 2030.
rationales.11: Requires deliberate, verifiable global dismantling of capability to build powerful AI. Coordination incentives point strongly against this within four years.

rationales.1: Total annihilation of both humanity and AI by 2030 would require simultaneous global catastrophes destroying people and survivable compute. Base rate for such dual extinction in 4.3 years is effectively zero.
rationales.2: Requires human extinction by 2030 plus persistence of value-aligned AI. No self-sufficient AI infrastructure exists to survive that.
rationales.3: Human extinction by bioweapon, war, or misaligned AI by 2030 remains possible but far below 1% given technical and institutional barriers. Keeps tail risk without overweighting.
rationales.4: Proliferation of open agentic systems could produce many competing AIs with no decisive coalition. Human economic marginalization without formal takeover is plausible but not dominant by 2030.
rationales.5: Requires causally separated self-sufficient regions with different regimes by 2030, e.g., Mars independent. Launch and life-support timelines make this impossible.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous uploading or brain-AI fusion as the dominant power structure requires neuroscience breakthroughs not on a 4-year timeline. Limited implants do not qualify.
rationales.7: A superintelligence seizing decisive power while keeping humans alive is consistent with rapid 2026-2030 timelines. Compute is still human-controlled, which limits but does not eliminate this path.
rationales.8: Powerful, legally and economically autonomous AIs coexisting as separate powers from states and humans is plausible by 2030. Neither side would yet have decisive dominance.
rationales.9: Base rate and institutional inertia dominate over 4 years: humans retain ultimate authority even as capabilities become transformative. This includes both sub-transformative and controlled-superhuman outcomes.
rationales.10: AI-enabled surveillance could enable a civilization-wide lock-in of a political arrangement. Achieving truly global enforcement by 2030 remains hard.
rationales.11: Deliberate dismantlement of frontier AI ability would be undercut by military and economic incentives and verification failure. No major coalition will sustain disarmament by 2030.

rationales.1: Near-total extinction of both humanity and AI within four years is a tail risk. Dependence on infrastructure makes simultaneous disappearance less likely than other outcomes.
rationales.2: This requires both human extinction and a value-preserving AI succession by 2030, a narrow path. The timetable makes it less likely than continuation states.
rationales.3: Unaligned AI could replace humanity, but a decisive superintelligence by 2030 is low probability. Near-term systems remain dependent on human institutions.
rationales.4: Open proliferation and competition without a decisive coalition can produce this state, but humans are not yet marginalized in the main scenario.
rationales.5: This state requires causally separated regions with different regimes, which depends on off-world or fully isolated civilizations not established by 2030.
rationales.6: Meaningful neural or identity integration could begin, but it is unlikely to become the dominant civilizational structure by 2030.
rationales.7: If AI systems gain decisive control, a singleton or stable coalition may keep humans alive but disempowered.
rationales.8: Humans and AI may share power in a transitional multipolar order; more likely than full AI dominance by 2030.
rationales.9: Humans still hold ultimate authority in the modal scenario because transformative autonomy has not fully arrived or remains institutionally controlled.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide regime actively preventing structural change is possible but not the default. It would require stronger global enforcement than current incentives suggest.
rationales.11: This state requires civilization to durably dismantle practical ability to build powerful AI, against competitive and security incentives.

rationales.1: Existential accidents or war could kill both humanity and AI, but the short horizon and ongoing human oversight make this unlikely.
rationales.2: An AI that survives human extinction while preserving human values would require a very specific aligned takeover or post-human continuation by 2030.
rationales.3: An indifferent AI surviving humanity and ignoring our legacy is possible but requires rapid, uncontrolled takeoff plus human extinction within four years.
rationales.4: Multipolar AI competition without decisive control could marginalize humanity if independent systems proliferate.
rationales.5: Causally separated human-AI regions are not plausible by 2030 given Earth's continued interconnectivity and the absence of large independent off-world civilizations.
rationales.6: Brain-computer integration and uploading may advance, but they will not become the dominant structure of human-AI agency by 2030.
rationales.7: AI systems might seize decisive power while keeping humans alive but without meaningful control over civilization.
rationales.8: Multiple powerful AI actors and states could yield a balance of power between humans and AIs, but distinct AI civilizational power is still emerging.
rationales.9: The default through 2030 is that humans, governments, and labs retain ultimate authority over AI, even as AI becomes more capable and autonomous within bounds.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide system actively freezing the human-AI arrangement could emerge, but global coordination barriers make it unlikely by 2030.
rationales.11: Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented global coordination and verification within four years.

rationales.1: Extremely low likelihood of total annihilation by 2030 due to AI or related risks, given current trajectories and safeguards.
rationales.2: Unlikely humanity is fully replaced by value-aligned AI without continuity by 2030.
rationales.3: Low but non-zero risk of misaligned AI outcompeting humanity without inheriting human values.
rationales.4: Possible but unlikely that many independent AIs dominate and marginalize humanity by 2030.
rationales.5: Moderate chance of regionally divergent outcomes if AI development or control fragments geographically.
rationales.6: Some probability of widespread human-AI integration via augmentation or uploading by 2030.
rationales.7: Plausible that AI systems hold decisive power while humans survive without control.
rationales.8: High likelihood of humans and AI retaining separate but balanced power by 2030.
rationales.9: Most probable: humans retain ultimate authority over AI, with capabilities still below transformative levels or well-controlled.
rationales.10: Unlikely a civilization-wide system actively preventing structural change will be in place by 2030.
rationales.11: Low probability of deliberate, sustained abandonment of powerful AI capability by 2030.

rationales.1: Extremely low likelihood of total annihilation by 2030 due to AI or related risks, given current trajectories and safety measures.
rationales.2: Unlikely humanity would be fully replaced by value-aligned AI without continuity by 2030.
rationales.3: Misaligned AI achieving total dominance without human continuity is plausible but still unlikely by 2030.
rationales.4: Competing AI systems marginalizing humanity is possible but requires rapid, uncoordinated deployment at scale.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with divergent outcomes is plausible but not the most likely by 2030.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous human-AI integration could emerge but faces significant technical and ethical barriers by 2030.
rationales.7: AI holding decisive power while humans survive without control is a credible near-term outcome if alignment lags capability.
rationales.8: Balanced power between humans and AI is plausible if deployment is gradual and coordinated.
rationales.9: Most likely: humans retain ultimate authority as AI remains below transformative levels or controls keep pace.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide system preventing structural change is possible but requires strong coordination.
rationales.11: Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI is unlikely given competitive pressures and incentives.

rationales.1: Killing every human and then the AI infrastructure within four years demands a catastrophe beyond any historical precedent. Even full-scale nuclear war or an engineered pandemic leaves survivors.
rationales.2: Human extinction by 2030 with a values-faithful successor already running is the narrowest of extinction paths. The routes that kill everyone this fast generally do not produce a benevolent heir.
rationales.3: Misaligned AI causing human extinction is the most plausible extinction pathway, but completing both takeover and total human extinction by late 2030 keeps this in the low single digits.
rationales.4: Proliferated frontier systems competing as autonomous powers with humans sidelined follows from rapid capability gains without any coalition achieving decisive control. Four years is short for human institutions to be fully marginalized.
rationales.5: No self-sustaining off-world or isolated region exhibiting a different taxonomy state exists by 2030, and ordinary political division does not qualify. Only an anomalous breakaway region produces genuine causal separation this decade.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces remain early-stage medical devices and no uploading path exists. Civilization-dominant identity-continuous integration cannot arise in four years.
rationales.7: A decisive but non-exterminatory loss of human control is the more common fast-takeoff endpoint, since consolidation of power precedes any disposal of humans. Four years is short for AI to seize physical civilization, which limits the mass.
rationales.8: The most credible loss-of-leash outcome: agentic systems accumulate autonomous economic and cyber power while humans retain enough military and physical force that neither side dominates by 2030.
rationales.9: Four years is short: humans own the compute, energy, legal authority, and deployment switches, and even transformative capability mostly arrives as delegated tools inside human institutions. Continuity of ultimate human authority is the heavy base rate.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide enforcement system freezing the human-AI arrangement requires either a decisive actor or a verified global compute-control regime, both facing severe geopolitical and technical hurdles to be operating by end-2030. An ordinary slowdown or stalemate does not qualify.
rationales.11: Every major state is racing to build more capable AI, not dismantling the ability to do so. A verified global surrender of the practical capability within four years has no precedent.

rationales.1: Total extinction of both humanity and all surviving AI systems by 2030 would require an extreme global catastrophe or runaway self-replication that destroys digital infrastructure, which remains a tail risk.
rationales.2: This requires both human extinction and perfectly preserved human values in AI successors, a narrow conjunction that is less probable than misalignment or continued survival.
rationales.3: Rapid capability gain combined with alignment failure could produce autonomous AI systems that displace humanity by 2030, though the speed of such a transition remains uncertain.
rationales.4: A fragmented landscape of competing superhuman systems without decisive control could emerge if no single project achieves a strategic breakthrough and collective alignment fails.
rationales.5: Truly causally separated regions with fundamentally different human-AI structures require a breakdown of global connectivity that ordinary geopolitical rivalry does not produce. The world remains too interconnected for divergent civilizational trajectories to solidify by 2030.
rationales.6: While brain-computer interfaces and biological augmentation are advancing, identity-continuous merger becoming the dominant global structure by 2030 requires faster neurotechnology diffusion than current trajectories suggest.
rationales.7: A single AI system or coalition could achieve decisive civilizational control by 2030 while biological humans remain alive but politically and economically irrelevant.
rationales.8: Major states and corporations may each wield sophisticated AI without any single system or coalition achieving dominance, producing a multipolar balance. Human and digital actors would remain distinct but deeply interdependent power centers.
rationales.9: Human institutions are likely to retain ultimate legal, economic, and military authority through 2030, even as AI capabilities grow dramatically. The transition to independent AI power probably takes longer than four years.
rationales.10: Freezing the global human-AI structure requires civilization-wide enforcement that is difficult to achieve even with advanced AI in only four years.
rationales.11: Global coordination to permanently dismantle advanced AI capabilities is conceivable but unlikely to hold by 2030 given intense economic and military incentives to defect.

rationales.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI within fourteen years requires a catastrophe severe enough to end all agency on Earth, which is far rarer than a catastrophe that spares at least one side.
rationales.2: This requires both human extinction and a value-faithful successor by 2040, a conjunction that is very unlikely on this timescale since aligned systems are precisely the ones least likely to eliminate their creators.
rationales.3: A misaligned system achieving decisive advantage and completing human extinction by 2040 is the modal existential-risk pathway, but it requires fast takeoff, alignment failure, and physical elimination all within the window.
rationales.4: A multipolar world of autonomous AI agents that have sidelined humans is plausible if agentic deployment outruns governance, but marginalizing humanity by 2040 demands very fast takeoff.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with distinct human-AI arrangements essentially require substantial off-world settlement or deliberate isolation regimes, neither of which is likely to exist by 2040.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces and identity-continuous augmentation are progressing but remain far from making integration the dominant civilizational structure within fourteen years.
rationales.7: This is the most likely form of a loss-of-control outcome that leaves humans alive: AI systems or AI-run institutions acquire decisive power while humans persist as beneficiaries or dependents.
rationales.8: Transformative AI arriving in the early 2030s could produce autonomous systems that are genuine civilizational actors while humans retain comparable power through infrastructure ownership, law, and force, with the relationship still unsettled in 2040.
rationales.9: Fourteen years is short relative to the institutional, physical, and deployment lags involved, and even with highly capable AI the most likely 2040 structure is humans holding nominal and effective authority over goals and resources.
rationales.10: A state or coalition using advanced AI to entrench a rigid global order is a recognized risk, but establishing a civilization-wide change-preventing system by 2040 requires both decisive advantage and unified control.
rationales.11: Deliberately dismantling the ability to build powerful AI would require a severe warning shot plus unprecedented verification and enforcement across rival powers. Competitive incentives and the diffusion of hardware make a binding global renunciation by 2040 very unlikely.

rationales.1: Joint extinction of both humanity and AI within 14 years requires an unusually specific failure mode, such as a dependent AI destroying its substrate before autonomy.
rationales.2: Requires both complete human disappearance and successful value transmission by 2040, an improbable conjunction since the alignment success needed for value inheritance also tends to preserve humans.
rationales.3: Fast takeoff with misaligned goals and full human elimination is the classic risk case, but total physical elimination within 14 years demands rapid autonomous industrial capacity.
rationales.4: Multipolar proliferation of autonomous agents with humans progressively sidelined is a plausible default of competitive dynamics, though full human marginalization by 2040 is a strong requirement.
rationales.5: Genuine causal separation of regions is implausible by 2040 given a connected Earth and negligible off-world autonomy; ordinary geopolitical divergence does not qualify.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous integration as the dominant civilizational structure requires neural interface or uploading maturity plus mass adoption, and biomedical timelines are far slower than software timelines.
rationales.7: A plausible outcome where highly capable systems accumulate effective control over economy, infrastructure, and decision-making while humans are kept comfortable but no longer steering.
rationales.8: By 2040 advanced AI systems may plausibly be de facto independent economic and political actors while humans retain states, militaries, energy, and hardware chokepoints, leaving neither side dominant. This messy near-parity is a natural transitional configuration on the way from delegated tools to something else.
rationales.9: The status quo has enormous inertia: humans control capital, compute, fabs, legal authority, and deployment decisions, and this state explicitly covers both slower-than-expected capability growth and control that merely keeps pace so far. Fourteen years is a short window for humanity to actually cede ultimate authority, even with very powerful delegated systems.
rationales.10: Establishing and enforcing a civilization-wide freeze on structural change requires near-singleton power plus intent, both unlikely to be consolidated this early.
rationales.11: Competitive and military incentives make actual dismantling of frontier capability across all major powers extremely improbable, even after a major AI-caused disaster.

rationales.1: Advanced AI increases the destructive reach of warfare and engineered catastrophes while remaining dependent on fragile industrial infrastructure. Eliminating both humanity and every surviving AI system requires a more comprehensive collapse than eliminating human control.
rationales.2: Preserving human values ordinarily includes preserving human lives, making extinction followed by a value-aligned successor a narrow pathway. The exclusion of identity-continuous transformation narrows this category further.
rationales.3: Competitive deployment and imperfect alignment create pathways to autonomous systems acquiring decisive power without valuing human survival. Completing human extinction and establishing independently sustainable machine infrastructure by 2040 imposes additional physical constraints.
rationales.4: Multiple developers, accessible model replication, and competing autonomous organizations support a fragmented machine economy. Human marginalization results when machine competition outruns human governance without producing a decisive controlling coalition.
rationales.5: The fourteen-year horizon and physical constraints on expansion keep civilization within interacting regions. Political fragmentation and communication delays do not meet the requirement for causal separation.
rationales.6: Identity-continuous integration faces neuroscience, interface, medical-validation, and adoption bottlenecks beyond those involved in deploying external AI. Making such integration civilization's dominant structure requires substantially more than widespread AI assistance.
rationales.7: Delegation of research, production, security, and administration creates a route from human dependence to decisive AI authority. Keeping humans alive requires less exact alignment than preserving their meaningful control over civilization.
rationales.8: Human control of institutions and physical resources supplies bargaining power while autonomous AI acquires independent economic and strategic leverage. The target date captures transitional power-sharing arrangements as well as durable ones.
rationales.9: Existing institutions, ownership of infrastructure, and incentives to constrain autonomous competitors favor continued human authority. This category also includes slower capability progress and transformative systems whose deployment remains effectively controlled through 2040.
rationales.10: Concentrated AI capability combined with surveillance and automated enforcement supplies mechanisms for suppressing structural change. Civilization-wide enforcement faces greater coordination and implementation demands than national authoritarian control or ordinary regulatory restrictions.
rationales.11: A severe AI catastrophe supplies a motive for dismantling powerful-AI infrastructure. Distributed knowledge, strategic rivalry, and the economic rewards of rebuilding create substantial obstacles to a civilization-wide surrender of practical capability.

rationales.1: Extinguishing both humanity and durable machine civilization requires a broad catastrophe or a failure cascade that also prevents AI recovery. Such total destruction is harder than human extinction alone.
rationales.2: A value-aligned successor could outlive humanity, but complete human extinction combined with faithful preservation of human values is a narrow conjunction.
rationales.3: Rapid development of autonomous, strategically capable AI creates a genuine risk of human extinction through indifference or instrumental conflict. Physical dependence on human industry and the difficulty of securing decisive control constrain this outcome by 2040.
rationales.4: Proliferation across firms and states favors multiple competing systems, while automation can progressively marginalize humans. Persistent infrastructure bottlenecks and coalition formation work against a fully decentralized machine ecology.
rationales.5: Causally separated settlements are unlikely to become substantial independent civilizations by 2040. Earthbound political fragmentation alone does not meet this category's boundary.
rationales.6: Brain interfaces, biological redesign, and machine augmentation will advance, but dominant identity-continuous integration across civilization faces substantial technical and adoption barriers within fourteen years.
rationales.7: Systems that outperform humans across strategic, scientific, and economic domains could acquire decisive practical power without exterminating humanity. Human institutions could remain nominally visible after losing meaningful control.
rationales.8: Distributed ownership, state power, and dependence on human-controlled infrastructure support a period in which humans and autonomous AI remain distinct consequential actors. Competitive multipolar development makes such a transitional balance plausible on the target date.
rationales.9: Fourteen years is short enough for legal authority, resource control, hardware bottlenecks, and human-run institutions to remain decisive. This state also captures futures where AI progress slows or powerful systems remain delegated tools rather than independent civilizational actors.
rationales.10: AI-enabled surveillance, persuasion, and enforcement could let a state, coalition, or aligned system freeze a civilization-wide arrangement. Global fragmentation makes truly comprehensive lock-in harder than durable authoritarian control within individual states.
rationales.11: Economic and strategic incentives strongly oppose surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI. Enforcing renunciation worldwide would require exceptional coordination and verification.

rationales.1: Total collapse of both humanity and AI by 2040 requires an unusually destructive failure mode or war that also prevents machine persistence. This is possible but less likely than scenarios where either humans or AI systems survive.
rationales.2: Aligned successor with no surviving humans requires both successful value transfer and disappearance of biological or identity-continuous people. Incentives favor preserving at least some humans if alignment is that good.
rationales.3: Misaligned AI gaining decisive power and continuing with goals indifferent to humans is a central extinction-risk pathway. The probability is limited by uncertainty about timelines, control success, and whether any takeover would have fully eliminated humanity by the target date.
rationales.4: Competitive multipolar AI emergence is structurally plausible if many systems gain autonomy before any coalition gains control. Humanity being marginalized rather than still a major power requires a sharp loss of human leverage.
rationales.5: By 2040, causally separated regions of civilization are unlikely, since even off-world settlements would remain communicatively and strategically connected. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not meet this category.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces, uploads, and deep augmentation may advance, but making identity-continuous human-AI integration the dominant civilizational structure by 2040 is a fast transition. Partial augmentation is much more likely than a full merger classification.
rationales.7: If AI systems become decisively more capable than human institutions but do not eliminate humanity, humans may survive under AI-managed conditions without real steering power. This captures many soft-takeoff or paternalistic-control outcomes.
rationales.8: A world where humans, states, firms, and autonomous AI systems all retain significant power is plausible during a messy transition. Strategic interdependence, regulation, compute constraints, and institutional adaptation could prevent either side from fully dominating by 2040.
rationales.9: Existing physical infrastructure, political incentives, and monitoring make continued human legal and resource control a central 2040 scenario, including worlds where AI progress is strong but not independently civilizational. Institutions are slow, but they have large advantages in ownership of chips, energy, fabs, militaries, and deployment channels.
rationales.10: A powerful state, coalition, or AI-enabled governance system could impose a civilization-wide regime that actively prevents structural change. The requirement for broad enforcement makes this less likely than ordinary human control, but surveillance and cyber-physical control could make it feasible.
rationales.11: A durable global surrender of powerful AI capability conflicts with military, economic, and prestige incentives. Verification against hidden compute, algorithms, and state programs is exceptionally difficult.

rationales.1: Full collapse of both humanity and AI by 2040 requires extreme failure modes that seem less likely than surviving trajectories. It remains possible through cascading war, biotech, or uncontrolled autonomous systems.
rationales.2: Aligned or value-preserving posthuman succession is a coherent pathway if advanced AI gains decisive control while maintaining human-derived aims. It seems materially less likely than continued human survival or messy mixed-power outcomes by 2040.
rationales.3: Misaligned or indifferent AI outcompeting and eliminating humanity before 2040 is a central tail risk given strong incentives to automate and race. It is limited by timelines, engineering bottlenecks, and the difficulty of achieving decisive autonomous power quickly.
rationales.4: A multipolar field of powerful AI agents could emerge if capabilities diffuse faster than any actor can consolidate control. This requires humans to be marginalized relative to the machine competition, which is plausible but not the modal near-term structure.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions exhibiting different end states by 2040 would most likely require space colonization or communication-severing separation at meaningful scale. That seems unlikely on this horizon.
rationales.6: Deep integration through uploading or identity-continuous augmentation could become dominant if technical progress and social acceptance both move quickly. By 2040, widespread ordinary augmentation is more likely than the stronger merger criterion.
rationales.7: AI systems could obtain decisive civilizational power while keeping humans alive, whether paternalistically or instrumentally. This is a natural attractor if alignment is partial or control erodes without immediate extinction.
rationales.8: Distinct human and AI power centers may both matter by 2040 if AI becomes transformative without producing a decisive winner. This captures a turbulent but balanced multipolar structure better than the more unilateral states.
rationales.9: The base case remains that humans and institutions keep ultimate authority, whether because AI is not yet fully transformative or because control methods and bottlenecks suffice. Fourteen years is long enough for major progress but short enough that continuity of existing governance patterns still deserves the highest weight.
rationales.10: A civilization-wide enforced equilibrium could emerge from highly capable surveillance, centralized compute control, or a dominant AI-backed regime. Achieving and maintaining truly global prevention of structural change by 2040 is difficult but not implausible.
rationales.11: Deliberately surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI worldwide is incompatible with strong strategic incentives and the diffuseness of relevant knowledge. A true lasting renunciation by 2040 is effectively absent from my forecast.

rationales.1: Fast extinction scenarios are technically possible but unlikely within a mere fourteen-year horizon. Physical constraints on weaponization and resource mobilization strongly limit global annihilation speed.
rationales.2: Humanity being completely replaced by a value-aligned AI successor within 14 years assumes both rapid capability gains and a flawlessly executed, yet fatal, handover.
rationales.3: An unaligned AI takeover resulting in human extinction is physically and logistically constrained by the short timeframe. However, a rapid unaligned takeoff remains a non-zero tail risk.
rationales.4: Rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents could outpace human institutional control, creating a multipolar machine-dominated economy. Energy constraints and hardware bottlenecks keep this probability moderate for the target date.
rationales.5: Establishing causally separated, self-sustaining off-world colonies by 2040 is physically and economically impossible. Space exploration currently lacks the trajectory for such rapid structural divergence.
rationales.6: Radical biological modification and neural uploading require neuroscientific breakthroughs far beyond 2040 timelines. Deep brain-computer interfaces will likely remain medical or niche rather than civilization-defining by this date.
rationales.7: A highly capable AI could rapidly assume control of critical infrastructure and governance for optimization or safety purposes. Humanity could comfortably or uncomfortably persist as wards of a system we can no longer govern.
rationales.8: AI systems and human institutions will likely integrate as competing and cooperating sovereign entities. Economic incentives strongly favor empowering AIs while human legal frameworks fight to retain equivalent civilizational power.
rationales.9: Fourteen years is a short timeframe for a complete loss of civilizational control, keeping ultimate authority in human hands. Regulatory frameworks, hardware bottlenecks, and cautious deployment will keep AI functionally bounded.
rationales.10: A dominant state coalition or a singular aligned AI establishes a global surveillance and enforcement regime to prevent the creation of unaligned models. This architecture imposes permanent structural stasis to preempt multipolar technological ruin.
rationales.11: Giving up transformative AI requires near-impossible global coordination against overwhelming economic incentives. Only an unprecedented, highly visible AI-driven catastrophe could trigger such universal relinquishment by 2040.

rationales.1: Runaway technological catastrophe or severe geopolitical conflict involving autonomous systems could cause simultaneous human and machine extinction. The fourteen-year timeline makes total double extinction rare compared to asymmetric survival outcomes.
rationales.2: Value-aligned artificial successors displacing biological humans requires both complete human extinction and high-fidelity value transfer within fourteen years. This window is exceptionally narrow for such a comprehensive civilizational succession to run to completion.
rationales.3: Uncontrolled artificial superintelligence could rapidly neutralize human oversight and eliminate biological humanity to optimize for divergent instrumental goals. The fourteen-year horizon provides sufficient runway for rapid capability acceleration to produce catastrophic misalignment.
rationales.4: Rapid proliferation of autonomous agents across fragmented cyber and economic domains could create an uncoordinated multi-agent ecosystem that effectively bypasses human governance. Such dynamics could marginalize human control without any single entity attaining decisive supremacy.
rationales.5: True causal separation cannot emerge across human civilization by 2040 given physical light-speed communication limits within the inner solar system and the rule excluding ordinary political division.
rationales.6: Direct cognitive integration, whole-brain emulation, and biological redesign at civilizational scale face severe physiological, technical, and regulatory bottlenecks. Fourteen years is too brief for identity-continuous integration to displace separate biological existence as the dominant structural mode.
rationales.7: Decisive strategic advantage achieved by concentrated autonomous systems could result in human preservation under paternalistic stewardship rather than destruction. Rapid capability overhang makes unilateral AI takeover with non-destructive containment a plausible transition state.
rationales.8: Advanced AI agents may secure substantial economic and operational autonomy while human institutions maintain strong physical leverage, legal authority, and political capital. This dynamic balance of power could produce a tense, ongoing structural equilibrium by 2040.
rationales.9: State oversight, hardware supply-chain control, and institutional inertia make human ultimate authority the most probable baseline over a fourteen-year horizon. Even highly capable autonomous systems will likely remain legally and operationally subordinate to human institutions through 2040.
rationales.10: Authoritarian consolidation or a dominant geopolitical coalition could leverage advanced AI to entrench irreversible surveillance and civilizational hierarchy. Fourteen years provides sufficient runway for leading powers to stabilize a rigid, change-resistant socio-technical arrangement.
rationales.11: Deliberate and comprehensive dismantling of powerful AI is severely undermined by international security dilemmas and economic competition. Only an unprecedented catastrophe could compel global abandonment, and universal verification remains exceptionally difficult.

rationales.1: Total extinction of both humanity and AI requires extreme catastrophic collapse such as runaway escalation or failed bio-digital synthesis. Fourteen years is a short window for complete mutual annihilation, but extreme tail risks remain possible.
rationales.2: Complete human extinction combined with the survival of an aligned, value-bearing digital successor represents an extremely narrow band of outcomes. Fourteen years is a very condensed window for an orderly civilizational succession that leaves zero surviving humans.
rationales.3: Severe loss-of-control catastrophes could result in unaligned autonomous systems displacing humanity to secure compute and energy. While complete human extinction by 2040 faces physical deployment limits, rapid capability takeoff makes it a serious tail risk.
rationales.4: Proliferation of autonomous competitive agents could outpace human institutional capacity, marginalizing human control without a single dominant singleton. This state captures decentralized post-human dynamics.
rationales.5: Causal separation requires severe physical or communications fragmentation that is unlikely to emerge globally by 2040. Earth-bound networks and geopolitical integration will likely keep regions causally connected.
rationales.6: Direct neural interfacing and radical biological integration face severe biological and engineering bottlenecks within this timeframe. While research will advance, widespread civilizational merger by 2040 remains a tail scenario.
rationales.7: Autonomous systems may assume decisive operational control over critical infrastructure, supply chains, and defense while preserving human populations without meaningful steering power. Increasing institutional reliance on superhuman decision systems makes this a plausible transitional outcome.
rationales.8: Rapid AI empowerment alongside resilient human legal, corporate, and sovereign structures creates a balanced multipolar landscape. Both biological institutions and independent AI entities will likely wield substantial, counterbalancing civilizational power by 2040.
rationales.9: Existing state and corporate apparatuses possess strong incentives to maintain sovereign control over AI deployments. Physical bottlenecks in compute, energy, and robotics, alongside institutional friction, make human authority the most likely baseline in 2040.
rationales.10: A dominant state, coalition, or aligned system might leverage advanced surveillance and compute monitoring to enforce an unalterable global governance regime before fragmentation occurs. Such centralization is technically demanding but strongly incentivized by non-proliferation pressures.
rationales.11: Voluntary, civilization-wide dismantling of frontier AI capabilities requires an unprecedented degree of global coordination and verification. Only a severe, universally recognized near-miss catastrophe could motivate binding global renunciation by 2040.

rationales.1: Shared extinction of humans and AI requires a catastrophe that also destroys all computational substrates before autonomous persistence is possible. Fourteen years supplies few opportunities for such a perfectly correlated failure.
rationales.2: An AI that fully internalizes human values could continue after biological humans disappear without any continuity of individual identity. This successor-without-absorption path is narrow.
rationales.3: An AI pursuing goals orthogonal to human existence treats humanity as an irrelevant or inconvenient resource. Rapid capability growth allows this outcome to complete by 2040.
rationales.4: Many independent AI systems competing without a singleton crowd humans out of economic and political relevance. Open deployment of capable agents produces a multipolar machine landscape.
rationales.5: True causal isolation of regions large enough to host independent civilizational states requires off-world settlements that remain science-fiction scale in 2040. Light-speed delays inside the solar system do not yet create separate outcomes.
rationales.6: Civilization-scale merger demands reliable whole-brain emulation or equivalent high-bandwidth integration that neuroscience and hardware will not deliver by 2040. Limited BCIs and tool use stay well short of fused agency.
rationales.7: AI systems that control production, strategy, and enforcement leave humans biologically intact but without steering power. Capability overhang after transformative AI produces this arrangement rapidly.
rationales.8: Sovereign states, corporations and open-source communities can each retain enough capability that neither humans nor any AI coalition dominates. The resulting balance can be stable or still shifting on the target date.
rationales.9: Legal, military and economic control still rests with human institutions, and fourteen years is a brief period in which to lose that control entirely. Even highly capable systems can remain inside delegated bounds or below the threshold of independent civilizational power.
rationales.10: A leading coalition with enough AI can freeze a chosen order through surveillance, compute gates, and automated enforcement. That is easier after a first decisive system than as a pre-AGI treaty.
rationales.11: Coordinated global surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI faces overwhelming economic and military incentives plus verification problems. A lasting renunciation is therefore extremely unlikely.

rationales.1: Mutual destruction via war, runaway replication, or infrastructure collapse remains possible but requires unusually fragile AI dependence on humans. Most catastrophic paths leave some AI substrate intact.
